title: Why I hate popsicle sticks for cold calling
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes challenges the familiar classroom routine of drawing named popsicle sticks to decide who answers a question. She supports cold calling but argues that random selection cannot tell a teacher who should be heard, what they are trying to find out, or what to do with the answer. Her alternative is purposeful selection, informed by first gathering responses from everyone through mini-whiteboards, partner talk, or written answers and then choosing a speaker for a reason. She also warns that the suspense of the draw can displace thinking, and she stresses giving wait time before calling on anyone. Citing EEF guidance and the Embedding Formative Assessment trial, she concludes that random selection may sometimes suit the moment but should never be mistaken for a teaching decision.
points: Equal odds of being picked are not the same as an equal opportunity to show what you know.
Hughes wants evidence from the whole class before choosing whose answer to hear, so the choice can surface an error or model a useful explanation.
For some pupils the suspense of the random draw becomes more prominent than the question itself.
Mary Budd Rowe's wait-time research supports putting thinking time before any cold call.
The EEF's Embedding Formative Assessment trial, across 140 schools, produced two months' additional progress by gathering answers from all pupils.
quotes: I have nothing against popsicles or lolly ices as all right-thinking northerners call them. It’s the sticks in the classroom I object to.
a name pulled from a cup doesn’t tell me who I should hear from, what I’m trying to find out, or what I’ll do with the answer. And those are the questions that make cold calling useful.

But purposeful selection and random selection aren’t the same thing. Purposeful selection means listening to what pupils have already said or written, noticing who has contributed recently, and choosing the next speaker because their response might help us take the learning somewhere.
It can give every pupil the same chance of being selected, but equal odds aren’t the same as an equal opportunity to show what you know.
There’s another reason I’m wary of the sticks: for some pupils, the suspense becomes more prominent than the question. They’re waiting to see whose name comes out, not thinking about the answer.
The EEF’s Embedding Formative Assessment trial involved 140 English schools and around 25,000 pupils. The programme led to two months’ additional progress on average
